work.title: VISUAL LITERACY
work.subtitle: 视觉阅读课程
work.scope: Fictional adult learning exercises. Illustrations are not records of real participants or research evidence. No accredited qualification or actual learner outcomes are supplied.

pages.title: Read an image in layers.
pages.lead: This course treats visual reading as a sequence of description, attention and interpretation. The illustrations are authored images, not documentary evidence of real places.
pages.body: Start with what is present, then ask how it is arranged, then consider possible meanings. Keep those three layers visible in your notes.
pages.detail: Working record: Describe the classroom image in three sentences, one for each layer. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Describe the classroom image in three sentences, one for each layer.

pages.title: Mark the composition.
pages.lead: Locate the largest shapes and their relationship to the frame. Describe position and proportion in ordinary language rather than claiming exact measurements from a stylised illustration.
pages.body: A bright table may sit low in the frame while a dark wall forms the background. The contrast can guide attention without proving which object matters to the people shown.
pages.subheading: Foreground / middle ground / background / focal area
pages.detail: Working record: Sketch a simple composition map using no more than five labelled shapes. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Sketch a simple composition map using no more than five labelled shapes.

pages.title: Build a colour vocabulary.
pages.lead: Name hue, relative lightness and contrast separately. A colour description is more precise when it explains a relationship instead of assigning a universal mood.
pages.body: Cobalt blue beside mustard yellow creates a strong visible contrast. Calling that contrast cheerful is an interpretation that another viewer may not share.
pages.detail: Working record: Describe two colour relationships and label any emotional association as your interpretation. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Describe two colour relationships and label any emotional association as your interpretation.

pages.title: Trace the order of attention.
pages.lead: Record where you looked first, second and third, then ask which visible features might explain that route. Your viewing order is a personal observation, not a population result.
pages.body: A pale sheet against a dark tabletop may attract attention through contrast. Another reader may notice a face first. Neither route is a measured general rule.
pages.subheading: First noticed / next noticed / visible cue
pages.detail: Working record: Write your attention sequence and compare it with a second possible route. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Write your attention sequence and compare it with a second possible route.

pages.title: Distinguish object from symbol.
pages.lead: An object can support more than one symbolic reading. Connect a proposed meaning to the image and its context rather than treating a symbol as a fixed dictionary entry.
pages.body: An open notebook might suggest learning, unfinished work or simply a useful tabletop object. The image alone does not decide among those readings.
pages.subheading: Object / possible meaning / supporting clue / uncertainty
pages.detail: Working record: Offer two readings of one object without selecting a definitive meaning. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Offer two readings of one object without selecting a definitive meaning.

pages.title: Compare two visual choices.
pages.lead: Use the same comparison dimensions for both images. A consistent comparison is easier to inspect than a sequence of personal preferences.
pages.body: Compare where the brightest area appears, how figures are grouped and which edges are cropped. Avoid turning a compositional difference into a claim about actual behaviour.
pages.subheading: Dimension / image A / image B / interpretation
pages.detail: Working record: Complete a three-row comparison using composition, contrast and grouping. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Complete a three-row comparison using composition, contrast and grouping.

pages.title: Ask where the image came from.
pages.lead: Record authorship, production method and what the source actually supplies. These case illustrations are AI-generated editorial images, with individual provenance listed alongside the document.
pages.body: A source note establishes how an asset was selected; it does not establish that the depicted lesson took place. Keep illustration provenance separate from claims about a real subject.
pages.subheading: Asset / production method / source note / evidence limit
pages.detail: Working record: Write a caption that identifies an illustration without presenting it as a photograph of an event. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Write a caption that identifies an illustration without presenting it as a photograph of an event.

pages.title: Name the edge of interpretation.
pages.lead: List what cannot be established from the image. Being explicit about the boundary makes a visual analysis more useful, not less imaginative.
pages.body: Attendance, accessibility, learning outcomes and relationships between the figures are not supplied by the illustration. These would require relevant independent information.
pages.detail: Working record: Choose one tempting claim and name the source that would be needed to examine it. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Choose one tempting claim and name the source that would be needed to examine it.

pages.title: Compose a short visual analysis.
pages.lead: Bring description, arrangement and interpretation into a compact paragraph. Mark the transition between an observable feature and your proposed reading.
pages.body: A useful sentence might begin The bright table contrasts with the darker wall, followed by I read this as a focus on shared work. The wording keeps the interpretation attributable to the reader.
pages.detail: Working record: Write a short analysis with one clearly marked interpretive sentence. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Write a short analysis with one clearly marked interpretive sentence.

pages.title: Keep a visual reading archive.
pages.lead: Save the source note, composition map, comparison and final analysis together. The archive records your reading process rather than certifying a correct interpretation.
pages.body: Use an earlier and later caption to show how your language became more precise. Record one question that the images could not answer.
pages.detail: Working record: Choose one sentence whose evidence boundary became clearer and explain the revision. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Choose one sentence whose evidence boundary became clearer and explain the revision.
